items.title: Behind AI industry’s call for independent reviews, a fight over what gets made public: Reuters exclusive
items.description: Anthropic and OpenAI have sought significant control over what outside evaluators can publish, concerned that findings could reveal trade secrets.

items._ogDesc: Anthropic and OpenAI have sought significant control over what outside evaluators can publish, concerned that findings could reveal trade secrets.
items.body:
NEW YORK — Anthropic and OpenAI have sought significant control over what outside evaluators can publish, concerned that findings could reveal trade secrets, according to two people familiar with the discussions.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said last month that external evaluators should have the right to publish key findings “without editorial control.” OpenAI agreed days later, saying assessors should have “editorial independence.”

The AI companies are worried that evaluator staff working inside the companies’ walls as part of so-called embedded evaluation could take proprietary information to rivals, according to the people, who declined to be named as the matter was private.

  • Latest updates on artificial intelligence news here

Measures under discussion to prevent intellectual-property leaks include having lab employees observe embedded teams as they work and preventing evaluators embedded at one lab from working at another simultaneously, one of the people added.

But what labs consider crucial intellectual property can overlap with information relevant to judging a model’s risk, which can lead to arguments and redactions, said a separate person with knowledge of past dealings with the labs.

Experts have said independence of evaluators is a concern as Anthropic and OpenAI choose who gets to carry out the reviews. Reuters is reporting details of these negotiations between the evaluators and the AI labs for the first time.

The discussions highlight the tension between a need to make the world aware of powerful and potentially dangerous AI and demands to safeguard trade secrets by AI companies seeking trillion-dollar valuations in what could be major IPOs.

The outcome of the talks will help determine how the world scrutinizes a technology that some of its creators warn may be advancing beyond humanity’s ability to manage.

Without agreed standards and legislation for independent reviews, some experts said the companies building the most powerful AI models could dictate how their systems are examined, leaving evaluators at the mercy of the labs themselves.

Negotiations over publication rights

The nature of the discussions changed quickly. The two people with knowledge of the matter said that as recently as October 5, Anthropic and OpenAI were seeking strict editorial control over what the evaluators could publish. By October 8, talks between Anthropic and some evaluators appeared to have evolved, according to one person familiar with the matter.

In response to questions from Reuters, Anthropic said that seeking significant control over embedded evaluators’ publications did not accurately characterize all of its discussions and work with independent evaluators.

  • Latest technology news on BNNBloomberg.ca

The company behind the Claude AI models said that, in current conversations with evaluators it previously worked with, it had made clear that the outside reviewers control their methods, evaluation criteria, conclusions and what to publish.

For new evaluator firms, Anthropic said it reserved the right to comment on and approve reports as the reviewers learn how its models operate and establish a working relationship.

OpenAI, for its part, said it was not seeking approval rights over the full text of reports produced by evaluators. It said its standard practice is to redact confidential information, and evaluators can disclose whether major redactions were made.

The ChatGPT maker said last month that AI labs and assessors should agree on the scope and access before testing, disclose methods and conflicts, and let assessors control their findings, while allowing labs to protect sensitive information.

The language AI labs already use in certain contracts with firms that evaluate their models can bar those firms from publishing confidential information in their reports without the companies’ consent, according to a contract seen by Reuters.

Promises of independence

Anthropic last month said that Faculty, Accenture’s specialist AI business, would be its first embedded evaluator, but said details on what evaluators can access and how they report findings were still being worked out.

“Evaluators are only useful if people can trust what they report, so independence and transparency are critical,” Faculty CEO Marc Warner told Reuters.

Technology companies typically bar the firms they work with from sharing such information with others without their consent.

But experts said the stakes are higher with AI, technology that, according to its developers, will have major implications for humans.

The labs could control the access evaluators depend on in the absence of standards, giving them leverage over what gets reported, Rumman Chowdhury, former US Science Envoy for AI under the Biden administration and CEO of Humane Intelligence PBC, told Reuters.

“Evaluators have this very privileged access, but whether explicitly or implicitly, they know that it comes at a cost,” Chowdhury said.

  • Latest updates on company news here

Independent evaluation was one of four safety measures in the one-page White House Accord on Super Intelligence, signed by U.S. President Donald Trump and leading AI executives late last month. But the accord, which Trump has called “morally binding,” did not say how those reviews should be conducted.

Evaluators also issued their own minimum conditions last month in a public letter that has been signed by more than 200 researchers, including Geoffrey Hinton, one of the godfathers of AI. The letter calls for independent control of findings, broad access to AI labs and protection from retaliation.

Redactions and restricted access

OpenAI redacted nonpublic information from a report by Model Evaluation and Threat Research, or METR, and Redwood Research on the Hugging Face incident, in which autonomous agents powered by OpenAI’s advanced models went rogue and set off a hack that compromised Hugging Face’s infrastructure.

The AI safety nonprofits’ investigation, first planned as two days at OpenAI, stretched to six days over three visits, with a more complete set of transcripts arriving only on the last one, after the researchers flagged gaps in the data.

METR and Redwood said they edited the report’s structure, emphasis, clarity and tone based on OpenAI’s feedback, but that nothing else important to their conclusions was removed. They stood by their findings and praised the access OpenAI ultimately provided, but said the risk of deterring developers from bringing in outside evaluators after serious incidents shaped their judgment calls in drafting, editing and redacting the report.

Reporting by Aditya Soni in New York; Editing by Kenneth Li and Matthew Lewis

items.title: Anthropic warns of AI ‘worms’ spreading across smart gadgets
items.description: Small artificial intelligence models may be only months away from being able to behave like a computer worm, copying themselves from one internet-connected gadget to the next without human help, AI giant Anthropic said.

items._ogDesc: Small artificial intelligence models may be only months away from being able to behave like a computer worm, copying themselves from one internet-connected gadget to the next without human help, AI giant Anthropic said.
items.body:
Small artificial intelligence models may be only months away from being able to behave like a computer worm, copying themselves from one internet-connected gadget to the next without human help, AI giant Anthropic said.

The finding potentially opens a new front in the cybersecurity threats emerging from AI, which have rattled governments and the companies rushing to adopt the technology.

The research, posted on an Anthropic blog late Monday, comes as tech companies race to build ever more powerful AI directly into phones, laptops, cars and household devices, rather than running it only in distant data centres.

A computer worm is malicious software that spreads between machines on its own. Researchers at Anthropic said an AI version would no longer need powerful data centers to operate.

Instead, it could run on networks of cheap, poorly secured consumer devices such as smart TV boxes and kitchen appliances.

The researchers modeled their estimate on Kimwolf, a botnet -- a network of hijacked devices controlled by hackers -- that infected more than two million devices at its peak, mostly off-brand Android TV boxes.

An AI worm of this kind would likely be slow, taking days to copy itself, William Zhou and Daniel Freeman of Anthropic said, comparing it to a slime mold or a swarm of fruit flies.

But once created, it would be hard to stamp out, because there would be no central switch to turn off.

The researchers said their estimate was rough, since it was based on one type of gadget and one past botnet.

But over time, the amount of computing power sitting in everyday gadgets is expected to keep growing, while the AI models needed to pull this off are likely to keep getting smaller, the researchers added.

items._ogDesc: Domino’s Pizza scaled back its full-year sales outlook, warning that U.S. and international comparable sales growth would remain muted.
items.body:
Domino’s Pizza on Tuesday scaled back its full-year sales outlook, warning that U.S. and international comparable sales growth would remain muted, sending shares down about 3 per cent in early trading.

The pizza giant has reported slowing comparable sales for several quarters running, squeezed by rising competition, persistent inflation and a softening US labor market that have made consumers increasingly cautious about discretionary spending.

  • Latest updates on company news here

Here are some details:

  • “We expect the macro environment to remain an overhang on the consumer through the balance of the year,” CEO Joe Jordan, who joined earlier this month, said on a post earnings call
  • Demand remains challenging across the quick-service restaurant and pizza industry, Jordan added.
  • Jordan said the company aims to restore profit and order-count growth while expanding its competitive reach beyond the traditional quick-service pizza market.
  • Domino’s now expects US same-store sales to be towards the low end of low-single-digit growth forecast.
  • The key test for the new CEO is driving order growth through promotions and new products without hurting franchisee profitability, said Lale Akoner, an analyst at eToro.
  • Its annual international comparable sales are expected to be about flat, compared with prior forecast of low-single-digit growth.
  • Domino’s posted quarterly US same-store sales growth of 0.3 per cent, below analysts’ estimates of a 0.71 per cent rise, according to data compiled by LSEG.
  • Its quarterly international same-store sales grew 0.2 per cent, versus estimates of 0.88 per cent rise.
  • However, Domino’s posted quarterly revenue of US$1.19 billion and profit of US$4.60 per share, both topping estimates of US$1.18 billion and US$4.37 per share, respectively.

Reporting by Anuja Bharat Mistry in Bengaluru; Editing by Tasim Zahid

items._ogDesc: Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre will be in Detroit on Tuesday to make a case for tariff-free trade in the auto sector.
items.body:
OTTAWA — Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre will be in Detroit on Tuesday to make a case for tariff-free trade in the auto sector.

At a news conference in Windsor, Ont. before crossing into the United States, Poilievre said he planned to meet with representatives of a General Motors plant in Detroit and officials from a Ford plant in nearby Dearborn, Mich.

He is also planning to meet with members of the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers while in Michigan.

Poilievre said he will be joined by members of the Conservative caucus from the Windsor area.

The Conservative leader blamed the trade war for declining auto production on both sides of the border.

“The story is not rosy there either and that is because of this ridiculous trade war that is only helping China and other overseas competitors. We should not be fighting with each other while our risks and rivals abroad get stronger,” Poilievre said.

The trade war has emerged as a major factor in the U.S. midterm election race in Michigan, the heart the of the U.S. auto industry.

Despite having previously supported U.S. President Donald Trump’s tariffs, Michigan Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers released a video last week saying “Canada is not our enemy” and calling for an end to the trade war.

In a debate last week with his Democratic opponent Abdul El-Sayed, Rogers said he wants a deal with Canada and the current tariffs are too high.

The U.S. currently has a 25 per cent tariff on Canadian autos. President Trump has threatened to increase that tariff to 50 per cent on Jan. 1 in response to Canada’s counter-tariffs.

When asked about Trump’s adviser Peter Navarro recently warning that Canada would pay a price for any interference in the midterm elections, Poilievre said he doesn’t see his visit ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm vote as meddling.

“I think we’re going there to fight for tariff-free trade on both sides of the border and Americans want lower prices and more jobs and we’re offering a plan for them to have both,” Poilievre said.

Trump ended trade talks with Canada last year after Ontario aired an ad during the World Series using clips of former president Ronald Reagan criticizing tariffs and supporting free trade.

In August, Prime Minister Mark Carney ordered the Canadian negotiating team to call off trade talks with the U.S. after accusing the Americans of making unreasonable demands.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 13, 2026.

David Baxter, The Canadian Press

items._ogDesc: Sharp drops for stocks in the computer chip industry are circling the world and hitting Wall Street, while strong profit reports keep the market unsettled.
items.body:
NEW YORK — Strong profit reports from Goldman Sachs, UnitedHealth Group and other big U.S. companies are helping to shore up the stock market on Tuesday, even as sharp drops for stocks in the computer chip industry circle the world and hit Wall Street.

The S&P 500 slipped 0.1 per cent to pull a bit further from its all-time high set last week, but the modest move masked big swings for stocks underneath the surface. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 300 points, or 0.6 per cent as of 9:35 a.m. Eastern time, while the Nasdaq composite was 0.4 per cent lower.

Some of the sharpest action was among tech stocks, where drops for chip companies dragged South Korea’s Kospi index down 5.5 per cent.

  • S&P 500 market updates here

Worries have been high for a while about whether chip stock prices have shot too high in the frenzy around artificial-intelligence technology, and concerns rose further following reports that China’s memory chipmaker CXMT is making advances that could challenge industry heavyweights like Micron Technology of Boise, Idaho and Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix of South Korea.

Micron fell 5.8 per cent and was one of the heaviest weights on the S&P 500. Nvidia slipped 1.3 per cent, Advanced Micro Devices fell 3.3 per cent and Broadcom slipped 1.3 per cent

Elsewhere on Wall Street, stocks swung after the first wave of big U.S. companies reported how much profit they made during the summer. Expectations are high, and companies will need to deliver strong growth to justify the record-breaking runs their stocks have made this year despite worries about high inflation, discouraged customers and the war with Iran.

  • Stay on top of your portfolio with real-time data, historical charts and the latest news on oil

UnitedHealth Group climbed 2.6 per cent after the healthcare company reported stronger profit and revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected. It also raised its forecast for profit over the full year of 2026.

Goldman Sachs was another winner and added 1.4 per cent after the bank delivered a profit for July through September that blew past analysts’ expectations. It benefited from strong growth for its business that offers loans to clients for trading stocks, even amid what CEO David Solomon called a “complicated operating environment” created by lots of uncertainty.

On the losing end of Wall Street was Wells Fargo, which reported weaker revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected. Its stock fell 1.2 per cent after CEO Charlie Scharf said revenue sank from its venture capital investments.

But he also said that “our data shows that our consumer and business customers are doing well” despite uncertainty about the economy and recent surveys showing how discouraged Americans are about the economy.

  • How to set BNN Bloomberg as your preferred source on Google

At the country’s biggest bank, JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon also highlighted “elevated asset prices” as one of the potential risks for the economy, a potential nod to the criticism that prices for investments have run too high. He also mentioned high inflation, rising interest rates and “geopolitical conditions,” among other challenges.

“These forces may be manageable, but we remain prepared for a wide range of outcomes,” he said.

JPMorgan Chase rose 1.2 per cent after reporting a weaker profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected but also giving a forecast for net interest income in the current quarter that topped Wall Street’s estimate.

In the bond market, Treasury yields eased after oil prices fell. The yield on the 10-year Treasury slipped to 5.20 per cent from 5.24 per cent late Friday. Trading in the U.S. bond market had been closed Monday for a holiday.

They benefited from a 1.3 per cent drop for the price of a barrel of Brent crude oil to US$105.22.

In stock markets abroad, Japan’s Nikkei 225 fell 1.8 per cent on weakness for several of its big tech stocks. Indexes were modestly higher elsewhere in Asia and across Europe.

Stan Choe, The Associated Press

AP Business Writers Chan Ho-him and Matt Ott contributed to this report.

This press release is provided by Business Wire and is published as received.

TORONTO--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- Markel Insurance, the insurance operations within Markel Group Inc. (NYSE: MKL), today announced the launch of its Contractors & Trades sector, providing brokers with a dedicated insurance proposition for contractors, trades and specialist construction-related businesses.

Building on Markel’s established environmental liability and property and casualty expertise, the new sector brings together casualty, property and selected specialist coverage within a coordinated underwriting proposition. The offering is designed to help brokers place multi-line contractors and trades risks through a more streamlined and clearly defined solution.

Markel’s initial appetite encompasses a broad but disciplined range of contractors, trades and specialist construction-related businesses. Further details are provided in the Notes to Editors section below.

The product scope includes Commercial General Liability, Excess Liability and property coverage, together with options for contractors’ equipment, tools and installation floaters. Depending on the individual risk and exposures presented, brokers may also be able to access specialist protection for pollution and professional liability exposures through Contractors Pollution Liability and E&O. Additional features may include business interruption, equipment breakdown, and selected coverage enhancement.

To complement the insurance proposition, Markel has partnered with ARAG Legal Solutions Inc. to provide policyholders with access to legal and risk management resources. These services include a legal helpline, contract review support, HR assistance resources, and a legal document centre.

“Contractors and trades businesses face a combination of operational, contractual, environmental and professional exposures that cannot always be addressed effectively through a standard insurance offering,” said Andrew Poulton, Vice President, Sectors. “Our Contractors & Trades proposition brings together our core casualty, environmental and property capabilities with specialist expertise where the exposure requires it. This gives brokers a clearer route into Markel, a broader package solution for suitable risks and an underwriting approach grounded in a defined and disciplined appetite.”

The launch reflects Markel Canada’s continued commitment to developing specialist propositions around the needs of brokers and their clients. The initial offering is focused on contractors and trades package business and is not intended to operate as a broad construction project or project-specific products solution.

For more information, brokers can contact their Markel representative or visit www.markel.ca.

items.title: Adoption of Samsara AI Agents Accelerates Across Physical Operations
items.description: Samsara Inc. announced the launch of Samsara Agent Studio, a no-code AI agent platform designed specifically for physical operations.
items._ogDesc: Samsara Inc. announced the launch of Samsara Agent Studio, a no-code AI agent platform designed specifically for physical operations.
items.body:
This press release is provided by Business Wire and is published as received.

SAN FRANCISCO--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- Samsara Inc. (“Samsara”) (NYSE: IOT), the pioneer of the Connected Operations® Platform, today announced the launch of Samsara Agent Studio, a no-code AI agent platform designed specifically for physical operations. Adoption on Samsara’s platform has accelerated 7x since June as customers expand AI from automating reports and uncovering fuel savings to anticipating compliance risk and reaching drivers through voice.

This press release features multimedia. View the full release here: https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20261013914021/en/

Agents built for knowledge work can wait for a prompt. In physical operations, much of the work is already moving, requiring agents to understand what’s happening in real time — and be smart enough to take action. Samsara provides that context through more than a decade of operational data on vehicles, equipment, workers, and sites including location, video, diagnostics, behavior, and environmental conditions, from customers across industries and geographies. Agent Studio turns that context into action, giving customers prebuilt AI agents and a builder for custom chat and voice agents tailored to their operations. Now available to all customers, it makes Samsara the first platform for physical operations to offer both.

“AI is quickly adopted when it’s useful, and in physical operations that means an agent has to understand the operation and meet people where the work happens,” said Johan Land, Chief Product Officer at Samsara. “In the back office that might happen through chat. On the road, it happens through a phone call. That is what brings an agent to life in the real world.”

From automating reports to anticipating risk

Agents built in Agent Studio are taking on work that once required hours of manual analysis or a dedicated specialist. Reporting is where many customers start, but adoption is quickly expanding into more complex work — finding opportunities to reduce fuel costs, predicting compliance risk before a violation occurs, diagnosing the cause of operational issues, and giving drivers immediate access to company-specific guidance.

That expansion is also happening within individual organizations. Deployed use cases include:

“We were spending more than six figures a year on reporting and data compilation, work that’s now fully automated,” said Derek Champagne, VP of Corporate Security, Asset Management & Housing at Grand Isle Shipyard. “The real benefit isn’t just efficiency; it’s the ability to focus our people on solving bigger problems, driving innovation, and creating value that simply wasn’t possible before.”

Voice becomes the primary interface for frontline workers

In physical operations, AI and its workers cannot depend on a screen to get a job done. A driver has their eyes on the road; a utility crew is repairing power lines. Voice gives agents an interface built for those environments — allowing workers to ask questions, receive instructions, and share information without stepping away from the work.

Customers are building agents that make and take phone calls, bringing live operational information and company-specific guidance into those conversations and extending support beyond the hours an office team can cover.

That can turn a physical event into an AI-powered workflow. When a truck crosses a geofence around an unfamiliar job site or distribution center, for example, a voice agent can immediately call the driver with site-specific instructions — which entrance to use, where to park, the yard speed limit and required safety equipment. The driver can ask follow-up questions using information from company policies and live operational data. When the truck leaves, the agent can capture details from the visit, while managers can use Samsara Assistant to analyze patterns such as which sites are creating the longest dwell times.

Across Samsara’s platform, voice has quickly become the dominant way people interact with agents. Within four weeks of launch, voice agents surpassed chat in interaction volume and have led every week since. Among organizations using voice agents, ~75% have increased their weekly usage since they began deploying them — more than half have at least doubled it.

“Start of Day Briefings help us get set for the shift, and two-way audio helps tackle drowsiness in the cab. It gives us the support we need in the moment to stay sharp, stay safe, and become better drivers,” said Tiny Kirby, a driver at Clyde Companies.

From understanding to action — wherever the work happens

For more than a decade, Samsara has built the technology to see and understand physical operations, now collecting more than 30 trillion data points annually from vehicles that traverse 99.9% of U.S. roads. Agents extend that foundation from understanding to action — and increasingly allow people to access Samsara’s operational context without sitting in front of a reporting dashboard.

Samsara’s agentic capabilities now reach people wherever the work happens:

Each draws on the same operational context and permission model, whether someone is talking to an agent on the road, working in the Samsara dashboard, or using another AI tool.

“Every day, our customers make thousands of decisions that determine whether people get home safely, deliveries arrive on time, and essential services keep running,” said Brendan O’Driscoll, VP of Platform at Samsara. “Our ambition is to make AI part of how that work gets done — anticipating what needs to happen and coordinating the people, equipment, and systems to act. That’s the future we’re building at Samsara.”

Agent Studio is now available to all Samsara customers. Watch the Agent Studio demo and learn more about the Samsara platform here.

Samsara (NYSE: IOT) is the pioneer of the Connected Operations® Platform, which is an open platform that connects the people, devices, and systems of some of the world’s most complex operations, allowing them to develop actionable insights and improve their operations. With tens of thousands of customers across North America and Europe, Samsara is a proud technology partner to the people who keep our global economy running, including the world’s leading organizations across industries in transportation, construction, wholesale and retail trade, field services, logistics, manufacturing, utilities and energy, government, healthcare and education, food and beverage, and others. The company’s mission is to increase the safety, efficiency, and sustainability of the operations that power the global economy.

items._ogDesc: UnitedHealth Group on Tuesday raised its 2026 profit forecast and indicated that Wall Street’s current estimate for 2027 earnings was too low, saying it would build on restrained medical-cost spending in its health insurance business and improved margins in clinical care.
items.body:
NEW YORK — UnitedHealth Group on Tuesday raised its 2026 profit forecast and indicated that Wall Street’s current estimate for 2027 earnings was too low, saying it would build on restrained medical-cost spending in its health insurance business and improved margins in clinical care.

The company has been in turnaround mode for the past two years after it suffered one of the biggest cyber attacks on the industry, missed financial targets and was forced to withdraw its outlook. It was also rattled by the killing of a top executive outside the company’s investor meeting in New York nearly two years ago.

UnitedHealth, which operates one of the largest US health insurance companies, clinical care businesses, pharmacy services and a pharmacy benefits manager, now expects 2026 adjusted profit per share of at least $20.50. That is up from its previous forecast of at least $19.50 to $20, and above analysts’ estimates for $19.86 per share, according to LSEG data.

  • Latest updates on company news here

For 2027, Chief Financial Officer Wayne Deveydt said the company is targeting the lower end of its long-term growth rate projection of 13 per cent to 16 per cent as a “reasonable starting point.”

“Current analyst consensus for 2027 may understate the opportunity ahead,” he said.

Wall Street analysts are estimating earnings of $22.61 per share for next year.

While UnitedHealth delivered a solid quarter, the real highlight was the continued durability of the margin recovery story, said Mizuho analyst Ann Hynes.

UnitedHealth shares were up 2.1 per cent at $386.61 in early trading.

On an adjusted basis, UnitedHealth earned $4.69 per share for the third quarter, up from $2.92 a year earlier, and well above the average analyst estimate of $4.14.

COST CONTROLS

UnitedHealth reported a third-quarter medical cost ratio — the percentage of insurance premiums spent on medical care — of 88.4 per cent, better than analysts’ estimates and the year-ago 89.90 per cent.

The company attributed the improvement to plan design and new pricing on products. It has exited some health insurance products this year and has named new top executives after missing financial estimates last year.

A $610 million reserve benefit reduced medical costs during the quarter, reflecting lower-than-expected medical cost claims for services provided earlier this year, the company said.

Revenue from its UnitedHealthcare insurance business fell to $86.3 billion from $87.1 billion a year earlier, even as earnings from operations and profit margins rose due to benefit changes, pricing, and medical- and operating-cost controls.

UnitedHealthcare operates Medicare Advantage health insurance plans for adults aged 65 and older and also runs Medicaid plans for low-income Americans on behalf of state governments.

The company said UnitedHealthcare membership declined in its employer-sponsored health plan business by 165,000 people due to attrition and that another 85,000 people left the Medicaid rolls due to eligibility changes.

Since the end of 2025, 935,000 members have exited its Medicare Advantage business.

Third-quarter operating income for UnitedHealth rose to $6.6 billion from $4.3 billion in the year-ago quarter, largely driven by improved operations in its Optum Health clinical unit.

UnitedHealth said technology investments, including on artificial intelligence, have reduced the overall costs of providing medical services. Optum also exited less favorable contracts for certain health plans that had dragged on earnings in the first quarter.

The company last year said Optum faced regulatory and cost challenges, representing an $11 billion blow to the unit over three years.

Overall third-quarter revenue of $112.69 billion beat analyst expectations of about $111.4 billion.

items.description:
As the October 26 Toronto mayoral election approaches, the city’s housing and affordability crisis remains one of the most pressing issues among voters, and for good reason.

Fewer than 1 in 6 Torontonians can afford to buy a home in the city, minimum wage workers have to work 145 hours per month to afford the average asking rent for a one-bedroom apartment, and while the city pledged to facilitate 285,000 new homes by 2031 in 2022, it’s only achieved 32% of that goal as of this August.

Toronto’s top mayoral candidates — Incumbent Mayor Olivia Chow, and former urban planner and City Councillor Brad Bradford —both say they can put a good dent in Toronto’s housing and affordability woes, but they differ on how to pull it off. Here’s how Bradford and Chow plan to tackle the housing file:

Olivia Chow

City-led affordable housing

Under Chow’s lead, housing has shifted out from under the domain of the private market toward a more public, city-led development model. Since Chow took office in 2023, 5,271 city-owned housing units have broken ground, including 1,680 affordable units. Her plan is to continue building affordable and rental units via her public development model, with a goal of delivering 65,000 rent-controlled homes by 2030. She also wants to encourage development through new incentive programs that cut fees for developers in exchange for affordable units.

Cutting red tape

Chow champions zoning reforms that allow for more missing middle housing, including as-of-right multiplexes, and fast tracking transit-oriented developments. She’s also working to streamline the development review process with pre-approved building plans and expanding the online application process with automated checks and submissions. Chow has said efforts like these have made Toronto 80% faster at approving new housing. She has also eliminated development charges (DCs) for projects up to six units, created an incentive program that eliminates DCs for purpose-built rental housing, and played a central role in securing the $1.5 billion tri-governmental deal to lower DCs by 40%-60% in June.

Protecting tenants

Chow has promised a $2.15-million bad landlord task force under RentSafeTO, if re-elected. The task force would use enforcement officers and lawyers to investigate reports of neglectful landlords and buildings in disrepair. Fines paid by landlords and RentSafeTO funds would pay for the initiative.

Expanding taxes

Chow says she backs increasing taxes on vacant and luxury homes to fund affordable housing and prevent speculation. It’s a stance she has been consistent on. In 2023, she created the luxury property tax and voted to increase the vacant homes tax from 1% to 3%.

Brad Bradford

Private development

Bradford disagrees with Chow’s public builder model for delivering affordable housing, favouring partnering with experienced non-profit and market builders who he believes can build housing faster and cheaper than the City has.

Cutting red tape

As the former Chair of the Planning and Housing Committee, Bradford brought forward the Housing Action Plan to legalize gentle density, update urban design rules like eliminating the angular plane, and speed up approvals. If elected, he promises to continue updating city guidelines and streamlining the development review process, in part by increasing the use of technology. Bradford has also long called for the dropping of DCs to get shovels in the ground faster. He put forward a motion to lower DCs by 25% last March, which was rejected by Chow, and voted in favour of slashing DCs by 40% or 50% this June.

Renter strategy

Bradford is proposing a three-part plan to help renters: “Keep your home. Cool your home. Build more homes.” He wants to keep the existing renoviction by-law, but improve its enforcement by implementing a public dashboard to keep track of licenses and investigations and provide more funding for enforcement. He also wants to ensure renters have at least one cool room in their house, without any rent hikes to pay for it. Finally, Bradford promises clearer rules and earlier funding for non-profit rental builders instead of one-off negotiations for each site.

No to taxation

Bradford is against raising taxes on vacant and luxury homes, and has said he wants to keep costs down for all Torontonians. If elected, Bradford also promises to eliminate Toronto's Municipal Land Transfer Tax for homes valued at or below $1.1 million.

items.body:
Time for your cheat sheet on this week’s top stories.

Canadian Real Estate

Canada Lost 110,000 Jobs Over Two Months, Wiping Out 2026 Gains

The narrative of Canada’s resilient job market has flipped in just two months. Employment fell by roughly 70,000 jobs in September, totaling a drop of 110,000 since August. The two-month slump was so sharp that it wiped out any year-to-date gains, putting 2026 in the red. Bearing the brunt of the downturn are entrepreneurs, public workers, and young adults. This seems to be an increasingly common theme in recent years.

Canadian Rents Fall For 24th Month, Driven By Shrinking Unit Size

The average rent landlords are asking fell for a 24th straight month across Canada. The average fell to $2,034/month in September, 4.2% lower than last year and 9.2% below the May 2024 peak. A breakdown reveals the data is heavily skewed by region and size. The drop in Ontario was enough to eliminate the continued surge in provinces like Nova Scotia. At the same time, more than half of the national drop can be explained by shrinking apartment sizes.

Canadians Continue Migrating To Alberta and BC, Flee Ontario

Canada’s great internal migration shows over 110,000 residents moved to a new province in Q2 2026. The biggest winner continues to be Alberta’s net gain of 5,893 residents in Q2 2026, making it the top destination. Ontario was on the losing end, with 7,063 more residents leaving than it gained from other provinces. Holding onto the bottom of the list for years now suggests Ontario’s problems are now systemic.

Toronto Real Estate

Toronto Home Prices Plunge To 6-Year Low, 28% Below Peak

The price of a typical home across Greater Toronto fell 0.9% to $917,600 in September, and now sit 28.3% below March 2022’s peak. Last month saw the second-weakest sales volume for September in over 15 years. Active listings also came in at the second-highest volume over the same period. The weak demand balance leaves the region in a buyer’s market, where prices are expected to fall.

Vancouver Real Estate

Vancouver Home Prices Hit A 5-Year Low As Buyers Pull Back

The price of a typical home across Greater Vancouver slipped 0.6% to $1.08 million in September, 5.5% lower than last year. The drop came with an 8.2% drop in sales, leaving volumes at levels rarely seen outside of a recession. Inventory tightened slightly, but remains at one of the highest September volumes. The persistently weak demand and strong inventory have pushed prices to a 5-year low.

items.description: Langley was the only market in the region to record year-over-year sales growth in September
items._ogDesc: Langley was the only market in the region to record year-over-year sales growth in September
items.body:
After a quieter summer, more homes came onto the Fraser Valley market in September, but buyers remain cautious despite declining prices.

There were 2,818 new listings in the region in September, an 18.8 per cent increase from August, according to the Fraser Valley Real Estate Board’s September market report. But the total was 18.2 per cent lower than a year earlier.

Sales totalled 922 in September, down two per cent from August and 4.2 per cent compared from September 2025.

“As buyers remain cautious and sellers face greater pressure to attract attention, subdued demand continues to weigh on home prices across the Fraser Valley,” the board said.

Benchmark prices continued to decline across property types in the region. The benchmark price for a detached home stood at $1.3 million, down 1.5 per cent from August and 8.8 per cent year-over-year.

The benchmark price for an apartment fell 0.9 per cent month-over-month and 9.3 per cent year-over-year to $461,800. Townhouses had a benchmark price of $745,300, down 0.7 per cent from August and 6.2 per cent from September 2025.

“For buyers who are in a position to act, this represents a significant shift in affordability and may create an opportunity for some households to move into a different segment of the market,” said Ishaq Ismail, chair of the Fraser Valley Real Estate Board, in a statement Monday.

Langley and North Delta saw stronger performance than some other cities in the region. Langley had 226 sales in September, up 3.1 per cent from August and 4.1 per cent from a year earlier. New listings rose 20.7 per cent month-over-month to 583.

North Delta recorded 39 sales, a 34.4 per cent increase from August, although sales were down 4.8 per cent year-over-year. New listings increased 32.5 per cent month-over-month.

Surrey had 1,124 new listings in September, a 15.6 per cent decline from July and a 17.8 per cent decline from August 2025. Sales edged up 0.7 per cent compared with August 2025 to 404.

In Abbotsford, new listings rose 24.5 per cent from August to 365, while sales fell 21.5 per cent to 113. Compared with September 2025, new listings were down 15.7 per cent and sales declined 18.1 per cent.

Mission saw new listings jump 42.3 per cent month-over-month to 148, while sales fell 9.4 per cent to 48. Year over year, new listings declined 13.4 per cent and sales dropped 22.5 per cent.

“A succession of economic shocks have conspired to weigh on consumer confidence, keeping many buyers on the sidelines,” said Anthony Boone, interim CEO of the Fraser Valley Real Estate Board, in a statement.

“Despite lower prices and more choice, buyers remain cautious, and that is being reflected in the pace of sales.”

Across the Fraser Valley in September, condos took an average of 46 days to sell, while single-family detached homes took 45 days. Townhomes took an average of 38 days to sell.

items.description: Five-year yields climb 20 basis points, raising mortgage costs before the Bank of Canada acts
items.content: <p>Five-year yields climb 20 basis points, raising mortgage costs before the Bank of Canada acts</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639271709111667971.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Five-year yields climb 20 basis points, raising mortgage costs before the Bank of Canada acts
items.body:
Canadian mortgage borrowers are already paying more for fixed-rate products — not because the Bank of Canada (BoC) has moved, but because bond markets have.

Five-year government bond yields in Canada have climbed 20 basis points over the past month, and any borrower renewing or initiating a fixed-rate loan today is absorbing costs the central bank has yet to formally set.

Canada’s path diverges from global bond markets

A global bond sell-off is driving yields higher across developed markets. The US Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) hiked rates 25 basis points at its September meeting.

The Federal Reserve Bank of New York estimates roughly 70% of the rise in US 10-year government bond yields reflects the resulting shift in rate expectations. Canada has not been immune, but the domestic picture is materially different.

RBC economist Claire Fan, who focuses on macroeconomic analysis for Canada, was direct about that distinction on the RBC Economics podcast The 10-Minute Take.

“The key difference here is that Canada’s economy is starting from a really relatively softer spot,” Fan said. “There’s still, by many measures, slack in the Canadian economy.”

That softness changes how the BoC can respond to inflationary pressure. With slack persisting in the labour market, Fan noted that businesses have less capacity to rapidly pass cost pressures on to consumers, giving the central bank more flexibility than the Fed when weighing inflation trade-offs.

Canada’s federal debt-to-GDP ratio is roughly half that of the United States and expected to trend sideways rather than climb, a contrast Fan said may yet drive divergence in bond yields between the two countries as domestic conditions reassert themselves alongside the shared global pressures driving both markets higher.

For borrowers, though, that divergence is still developing — and they cannot wait for it.

“For most households out there, it simply doesn’t matter why bond yields are rising. It matters that they are,” Fan said.

Fixed-rate clients are already feeling the squeeze

The distinction between the overnight rate and bond yields matters here. Floating-rate borrowers — those on variable-rate mortgages or lines of credit tied to prime — are insulated from bond market moves until the BoC acts. Fixed-rate borrowers are not.

Fan noted that the yield curve — the spread between longer and shorter-term borrowing costs — can drive fixed mortgage pricing just as consequentially as the central bank’s overnight rate, depending on the product and term a borrower holds.

Fixed-rate mortgages represent the majority of Canadian household borrowing, and those rates are moving now.

“Any borrowers these days, if they were to roll over their prior fixed-rate loan — so it could be a household rolling over or renewing their five-year fixed-rate mortgage, as an example — all of them will likely already be feeling the squeeze from higher bond yields, even before the Bank of Canada actually delivers those rate hikes that drove those bond yields higher,” Fan said.

With five-year Government of Canada bond yields rising sharply, renewal borrowers are facing a very different environment than the one that existed during the low-rate years of 2020 and 2021. https://t.co/GSUO3RkZUJ — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) October 8, 2026

For brokers managing renewal conversations, the pressure extends further than the current rate environment. The household debt service ratio is expected to edge higher into 2027, a concern Fan addressed directly on the podcast.

“For Canadian households, this does mean that some of the debt servicing reprieve that we’ve seen over the past two years has likely run its course, and the growth rate in debt payments will likely start outpacing the growth in household disposable income again. And that could potentially push the debt servicing ratio higher into 2027.”

Carrie Freestone, an economist at RBC in Toronto, summed up the dynamic on The 10-Minute Take: “Bond markets are essentially doing some of the Bank of Canada’s job for them.”

items._ogDesc: Canada lost 110,000 jobs in two months, wiping out 2026 gains. Public sector and youth employment fell as finding work became harder.
items.body:
Canada’s job market continues to stumble, erasing any gains made year-to-date. Statistics Canada’s (StatCan) September Labour Force Survey (LFS) shows a sharp drop in employment. Public sector workers and young adults carried virtually all of the pain.

Canada Lost 110,000 Jobs In Just Two Months

Source: StatCan; Oxford Economics.

The agency reported that seasonally adjusted employment fell 0.3% (-68.3k jobs) to 21.11 million in September. This follows the 41,700 jobs lost in August, adding up to a whopping 110,000 jobs lost in the span of just two months. The abrupt decline rolls back roughly 61% of the jobs added between April and July, leaving annual employment growth just 0.5% (+94.9k jobs) higher than last year. For context, the country’s population added roughly 189.4k over the 12 months ending September 1st.

The decline surprised the market consensus that expected 10,000 jobs to be added, according to National Bank Financial (NBF). “… the renewed strength in the labour market this summer may have been overestimated,” explains NBF Deputy Chief Economist Matthieu Arseneau and Senior Economist Alexandra Ducharme.

Canada’s Job Losses Are Mostly Public Workers and Entrepreneurs

StatCan notes the public sector lost 70,000 jobs in September, its fourth consecutive drop. The monthly drop more than accounts for the loss last month, the entire sector shrinking 2.6% (-118.7k jobs) in the past year. It’s unclear what share of last month’s drop was expected, as the end of Census 2026 was expected to reduce the size of the sector.

The agency also reported a loss of 22,500 self-employed workers last month, and 24,100 private sector jobs gained. The latter was “little changed,” according to StatCan, meaning it wasn’t statistically significant relative to the sector’s size.

Education shed 35,000 jobs, despite recent total enrollment data showing growth instead of an expected contraction. Education “often shows volatility at the start of a new school year,” notes Tony Stillo, Director of Canada Economics at Oxford Economics.

Healthcare and social assistance (-23,000) represented the second largest loss of any sector. However, the sector is far from hard hit—over the past year, it added 93,000 jobs against a national gain of just 95,000. Last month’s drop was the first it has seen since December 2022.

Youth Job Losses Lead, Work Gets Harder To Find

The vast majority of jobs lost last month were held by young adults, who represented 70% of the month’s net decline. Despite the loss, the youth unemployment rate remained unchanged at 13.0% in September. That’s exactly double the national unemployment rate, which also managed to only rise by 0.1 points.

NBF notes the national unemployment rate climb was relatively small due to the participation rate, which dropped 0.2 points to 64.8% in September. The population added 23,700 people aged 15 and older, but the agency reported 52,900 fewer in the labour force.

Employer layoffs aren’t hitting as hard as media reports may suggest, but it’s harder to find a job. StatCan reported the layoff rate remained near its pre-pandemic average. At the same time, their data shows just 30.6% of those unemployed in August found a job in September. In contrast, the ratio was 32.8% a year ago, and averaged 36.5% pre-pandemic.

Both NBF and Oxford Economics warn this report shows a weaker-than-expected economy. Arseneau and Ducharme argue the Bank of Canada “needs to exercise patience before raising rates,” additionally pointing to subdued wage pressure. On the flip side, Oxford’s Stillo sees a 25 basis point rate hike in both October and December, citing fuel-driven inflation risks.

items.title: Five-year fixed mortgage hits lowest share since records began
items.description: National Bank data signals a structural shift as Canadians move away from five-year fixed mortgages
items.content: <p>National Bank data signals a structural shift as Canadians move away from five-year fixed mortgages</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639271700468736684.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: National Bank data signals a structural shift as Canadians move away from five-year fixed mortgages
items.body:
Canada’s five-year fixed-rate mortgage has fallen to its lowest recorded share of new lending, according to a new National Bank of Canada report that points to a structural change in how quickly the Bank of Canada’s rate decisions reach household budgets.

“The five-year fixed-rate mortgage, long the preferred option for Canadians, has been losing ground for several years to shorter terms and, more recently, variable-rate mortgages,” said the Canada Watch research note authored by Daren King, senior economist at National Bank of Canada in Montreal.

Fixed-rate mortgages with terms of five years or longer fell to 8.8% of newly originated loans in July, the lowest level since records began in 2013, with the remaining 91.2% carrying shorter fixed terms or variable rates.

“In 2023 and 2024, borrowers primarily favoured shorter fixed terms, but these in turn lost ground in 2025 and 2026 to variable-rate mortgages,” the report said.

How the shift unfolded

The pricing backdrop has driven the change. Variable-rate products fell below fixed-rate options in late 2025 for the first time since 2022, according to Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC).

By February, variable-rate mortgages represented 42% of extended mortgages at chartered banks, consistent with broader industry analysis of how variable-rate mortgages could be set to surge in 2026.

Borrower sentiment followed quickly. Penelope Graham, mortgage expert at Ratehub.ca in Toronto, told Canadian Mortgage Professional that the momentum accelerated as rate cuts took hold.

“In 2025, borrower interest in variable rates rose as the Bank delivered additional rate cuts over the autumn months; on a year over year basis, the number of inquiries for variable-rate mortgages on Ratehub.ca increased by 25.7% year over year accounting for 11.5% of all inquiries, compared to just 7% in 2024,” Graham noted.

Separate platform data show variable mortgage demand rising while fixed products remained dominant at Rates.ca. The Bank of Canada has held its policy rate at 2.25% through multiple 2026 decisions.

What tighter monetary policy could mean for borrowers

The National Bank study identified a clear macroeconomic implication behind the shift.

“The more households opt for short-term or variable-rate financing options, the more quickly the Bank of Canada’s decisions are passed on to their mortgage payments,” the study said, adding that “the transmission of monetary policy could therefore accelerate compared to the past.”

That sensitivity cuts both ways. Should rate expectations tighten further, “a rise in financing costs could thus further dampen a residential market already grappling with modest activity and a less favorable demographic outlook,” the report warned.

For brokers advising clients on product selection, the shift reinforces the urgency of early rate risk conversations.

Canada’s outstanding mortgage stock has moved markedly away from its long-term fixed foundation over the past four years, a change that amplifies both the opportunities and the risks of the current rate environment.

items.title: What Canada’s top economists say about September’s jobs shock
items.description: The September jobs report just changed the rate conversation
items.content: <p>The September jobs report just changed the rate conversation</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639271683573879374.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: The September jobs report just changed the rate conversation
items.body:
Canada’s labour market lost 68,300 jobs in September, adding to an already discouraging August and pushing the national unemployment rate to 6.5%.

The Statistics Canada Labour Force Survey, released Friday, has produced near-unanimous agreement among five Bay Street economists: the Bank of Canada (BoC) is expected to hold its policy rate steady at its October 28 meeting, extending what most major institutions have long forecast as a rate hold through 2026 for Canadian mortgage brokers.

Two months of losses set the scene

Charles St-Arnaud, chief economist at Servus Credit Union in Edmonton, was candid about the bind facing Governing Council: “This adds to the BoC’s dilemma. On one hand, the economic outlook remains uncertain, with a weak labour market and a likely slowdown in growth in coming months due to the intensification of the trade war with the US. On the other hand, high fuel prices risk fueling broader inflationary pressures. As the BoC balances these, we believe it will opt for patience. As a result, we think the BoC will keep its policy rate unchanged for the rest of the year, unless there are signs in the CPI data of a broadening of inflation.”

Claire Fan, senior economist at the Royal Bank of Canada (RBC) in Toronto, urged caution in reading too deeply into the headline. “The monthly employment counts are notoriously volatile, and there are reasons not to read too much into the softer reading too quickly,” she wrote.

Fan noted that 70% of September’s decline, or 48,000 positions, came from workers aged 15 to 24, a group that “typically sees seasonal headwinds around this time of year after the school year starts.”

The unemployment rate, she added, “remained 0.6 percentage points below a year ago.”

Looking ahead, Fan said she expects the labour market’s earlier gains to hold: “We expect progress made in Canada’s labour market earlier will be largely sustained, and the unemployment rate to broadly edge lower through the end of 2026.”

What the data means for the October 28 BoC decision

Andrew Hencic, director and senior economist at TD Economics in Toronto, was direct on the rate outlook. “The labour market has now taken a breather for two consecutive months,” he wrote. “The top line job losses are disappointing, but the focus should be on the unemployment rate. An uptick in September brings it back to where it was in June.”

On market pricing and the near-term BoC path, Hencic added: “Ultimately, this report is going to pour some more cold water on near-term rate hike expectations for the BoC. Markets are currently pricing 27% odds of a hike in October, and 88% for December, the latter down from being fully priced yesterday. Given this backdrop we expect the BoC to remain data-dependent and stay on hold in October.”

Andrew Grantham, economist at the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce (CIBC) in Toronto, offered a more qualified read, separating data noise from structural risk.

“While the weakness in today’s employment data is likely more a reflection of data volatility than the impact of new US tariffs, the softness supports our call that the Bank of Canada will remain patient and keep interest rates on hold for now,” he wrote.

“Hours worked suggest a weak end to Q3 for GDP, and therefore a weak handoff to the fourth quarter as well, and it is possible that the unemployment rate could edge up a little further in the near-term due to job losses in tariff-impacted sectors.”

Dr. Sherry Cooper, chief economist at Dominion Lending Centres in Vancouver, pointed directly to the October 28 meeting. “The Bank of Canada will likely hold off on a rate hike, especially if the inflation data released on October 19 brings no nasty surprises,” she wrote.

On the global rate backdrop, a critical factor for Canadian fixed mortgage rates, Cooper drew a contrast between Canadian and American fiscal positions.

“Interest on federal debt alone absorbs 35.4% of all federal income-tax revenues stateside. A similar calculation for Canada is only 12.9%.”

Her message for Canadian mortgage professionals was plain: “Although Canadian bond yields are more than 100 basis points lower than in the U.S. for good reason, our yields typically move in the same direction as US yields.”

items.title: Home prices must plunge to fix Canada’s affordability crisis: CEO
items.description: With prices still about nine times average income, Canada’s market has a long way to fall
items.content: <p>With prices still about nine times average income, Canada’s market has a long way to fall</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639271637808645798.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: With prices still about nine times average income, Canada’s market has a long way to fall
items.body:
Canada is still facing a housing affordability crisis despite a market cooldown in recent years – and prices need to continue falling to give hopeful first-time buyers a fair shot at homeownership, according to a leading lending executive.

Fausto Gaudio (pictured top), president and chief executive officer of community credit union IC Savings, told Canadian Mortgage Professional that the affordability question far outstripped other problems facing the market including lack of supply and rising mortgage interest rates.

He said the continued inability of many working Canadians to qualify for a mortgage marked a “real structural problem” for the real estate market. “The major factor in what’s happening is the unaffordability of housing,” he said. “That’s really the underlying issue that needs to be corrected.”

The challenges facing the market have developed over decades: wages have risen only modestly compared with a massive surge in average home prices, meaning it’s become increasingly difficult for buyers – especially those purchasing for the first time – to put together enough money for a downpayment.

The average Canadian home price, Gaudio noted, historically sat at roughly 3.5 to 4 times average household income, a level widely regarded as a marker of a sustainable market. But that average ballooned to 12 times the average income at the peak of the COVID-19 housing market, and even in a cooler market has only slipped to approximately nine times.

“In order to get back to a traditionally healthy market, we’ve got to get back to that 3.5 times, from nine,” he said. “That’s a lot. That’s a big distance to cover.”

Market watchers are divided on the best way to achieve that. Housing minister Gregor Robertson stirred debate last year when he suggested home prices don’t necessarily have to fall to unlock affordability for more Canadians.

Others say lower interest rates would improve the picture for homebuyers, but Gaudio doesn’t see that idea as a surefire hit. “You drop interest rates, the price of housing goes up,” he said. “So we need to think a little more globally.”

‘The whole industry was closing an eye to this’

The wave of speculative condominium investment that defined the Greater Toronto Area (GTA) market in the years leading up to 2022 sent prices skyrocketing there, although condo values have plummeted by about 20% since then amid a deep market freeze.

Units, many measuring between 400 and 500 square feet, were built for investors anticipating capital gains on a sale or flip rather than for families or owner-occupiers.

A market that stopped functioning as a conventional housing market and more like a commodity exchange was an unwelcome development, Gaudio said.

“Because of all the investors that came into the market, it bumped up the demand curve to such an extent that real estate just went up and it became mostly one investor trading a housing unit to another investor, almost like a commodity,” he said.

He said the mortgage industry didn’t push back enough on that trend. “Mortgage brokers, mortgage lenders, the whole industry was closing an eye to this,” he said. “Very few people were speaking out and saying, ‘Where are we going? This is going to create an unsustainable market.’ And that’s what happened.”

Is the federal government’s approach to the housing crisis working?

Prime minister Mark Carney has introduced a range of measures to try to ramp up home construction over the past year and a half, including his flagship Build Canada Homes policy – a federal initiative to turbocharge homebuilding and ease the housing crisis.

That plan has been met with a mixed response, and some scepticism over whether it can meet its goals. Only around 2,000 affordable units of the 19,000 planned are currently under construction.

Gaudio, though, said the government is at least moving in the right direction on improving the housing outlook. “The governments are doing a good job in bringing more product to the market by subsidizing not-for-profit housing, affordable housing,” he said. “That’s a good thing. That’ll help to normalize prices.”

items.title: Canada’s job loss throws October rate hike into doubt
items.description: Back-to-back job losses hand the Bank of Canada a pivotal signal before October 28
items.content: <p>Back-to-back job losses hand the Bank of Canada a pivotal signal before October 28</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639271499118568386.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Back-to-back job losses hand the Bank of Canada a pivotal signal before October 28
items.body:
Canada’s labour market suffered its deepest monthly setback of 2026 in September, with the economy shedding 68,300 jobs. The result blindsided analysts and has reset the calculus ahead of the Bank of Canada’s October 28 rate decision.

Statistics Canada reported Friday that the unemployment rate climbed to 6.5% in September, back to where it stood at the start of the year. The country has now lost a net 41,200 positions in 2026, compared with net gains of 211,300 over the same stretch a year earlier. 

The figures follow Canada’s August labour market report, which shed 42,000 positions from the count, marking the first two consecutive months of net losses since the post-pandemic period.

Public sector bears the brunt

Educational services shed 35,000 positions and health care and social assistance fell by 23,000, together accounting for 58,400 of September’s losses.

Slower international student arrivals contributed to the education sector’s decline. Job losses were nearly evenly split between full-time and part-time workers.

The manufacturing sector, which carries partial exposure to American trade duties, declined by 12,700 roles.

Still, losses were not markedly concentrated in US-facing industries, a finding that points to structural and demographic forces as much as trade tensions.

Provincially, Québec recorded the sharpest decline at 49,000 positions, while Ontario and British Columbia each lost 20,000 jobs.

Alberta added 23,000 roles, the only major province to post gains.

The labour force participation rate fell 0.2 percentage points to 64.8%, its lowest level outside the pandemic era in 29 years. Statistics Canada attributed the decline to an ageing population exiting the workforce and fewer younger workers entering it under tighter immigration controls.

Carolyn Rogers says monetary policy alone cannot solve housing affordability, arguing that increasing housing supply and reducing the economy's reliance on rising home prices will require broader action from governments. https://t.co/j40csO7Yi1 — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) October 2, 2026

What this means for Bank of Canada

Andrew Hencic, Director and Senior Economist at TD Economics, was direct in his assessment of the September data’s implications for monetary policy.

“Ultimately, this report is going to pour some more cold water on near-term rate hike expectations for the BoC,” Hencic said.

“Markets are currently pricing 27% odds of a hike in October, and 88% for December, the latter down from being fully priced yesterday. We maintain the view that inflationary pressures are still relatively contained with average wage growth running at 2.4% and economic growth likely to slow further in Q4 as new tariffs weigh on activity. Given this backdrop we expect the BoC to remain data-dependent and stay on hold in October.”

CIBC earlier argued that the BoC rate hike case was weaker than Federal Reserve's due to the difference in their inflation problems. Meanwhile, UBS, Manulife, Oxford Economics and Scotiabank have expected an October increase.

Average hourly wages for permanent employees rose 2.3% year-over-year in September, up from 2.0% in August, a counterweight that the Bank of Canada’s policymakers will weigh carefully when the October 28 decision arrives.

The Bank has held its overnight rate at 2.25% through seven consecutive decisions in 2026.

items.title: Opinion: Canada’s housing crisis needs a new approach to ownership
items.description: Building more homes matters, but affordability also depends on financing, construction costs and creating realistic pathways into ownership
items._ogDesc: Building more homes matters, but affordability also depends on financing, construction costs and creating realistic pathways into ownership
items.body:
Housing affordability will inevitably dominate the political agenda as election debates intensify. For millions of Canadians, the question is whether they will ever be able to move from paying for housing to owning it—and building more homes will not solve that problem if they cannot get through the door.

The political response has rightly focused on supply. Canada needs to build more homes, and we need to build them faster. But after decades working across development, construction and investment, I have come to believe that the housing problem is not simply a shortage of buildings. It is a system that is not working well together. The way we build, finance and access ownership have become separate conversations, when they need to be part of the same solution.

The numbers show why. According to Statistics Canada in 2023, the median renting family under 35 had just $12,000 in liquid assets. Even if that entire amount were put toward a home purchase, the median family would still have been $80,000 short of a 20 per cent down payment. For renting families aged 35 to 44, the median shortfall was $97,000.

And the ability to close that gap is becoming harder when so much income is already going toward housing. StatCan found that in the first quarter of 2024, renters spent 33.3 per cent of their income on housing, compared with 22.8 per cent for homeowners. Renters also had negative net savings of $707 on average, compared with positive net savings of $2,835 for homeowners.

The barrier to ownership is not always the ability to make a monthly housing payment. For many households, it is the capital required to get into the market in the first place. StatCan has also pointed to the growing role of family wealth and inheritance in helping younger Canadians enter the housing market, raising the risk that the ownership gap becomes even harder to close.

That is the part of the housing conversation we need to change. Canada needs to innovate on both sides of the equation: how we build homes and how people access ownership.

On the supply side, Canada cannot build at the scale we need using a system that is slow, fragmented and expensive. Modern methods of construction can improve predictability, reduce waste and shorten construction timelines. But the objective should not simply be to build faster. It should be to create a more efficient housing delivery system, so those efficiencies can ultimately translate into more attainable homes.

The same thinking needs to apply to capital. Building a home is one challenge; getting the right capital into a project at the right time is another. Even when a home gets built, the traditional financing model can leave many Canadians on the outside looking in.

We need to think more creatively about how private, institutional, and impact capital can be structured to support attainable ownership, including new approaches to the upfront capital required to get into a home. This is not about replacing the mortgage or pretending that one new financing model will solve the housing crisis. It is about recognizing that the current system was designed for a different market. If the economics of housing have changed, we need to be willing to question some of the assumptions built into how we deliver and finance it.

Municipalities have an important role to play, too. Housing is ultimately delivered in communities, and local governments understand the land, infrastructure, workforce and economic conditions that determine whether a project can actually get built. They can help accelerate housing delivery by streamlining and expediting approvals, while working with builders, investors and other private-sector partners to test new approaches and identify what can be replicated at a larger scale.

That experimentation matters because there is no single Canadian housing market. The economics of building and owning a home in Vancouver are very different from those in a smaller community on Vancouver Island or elsewhere in the country. But the underlying problem is increasingly shared: people who can carry the monthly cost of housing are finding it harder to build equity through ownership.

We should therefore broaden what we mean when we talk about affordability. It is not only the monthly payment. It is the deposit, the financing structure, the cost and speed of construction, and the time it takes to deliver a home. Ultimately, it is whether a household has a realistic path to ownership. Solving that problem requires us to stop treating construction, capital and homeownership as separate problems. They are connected parts of the same system. If we can build more efficiently, deploy capital more effectively and create practical pathways into ownership, we have a much better chance of creating housing that is not just available, but attainable.

Canada absolutely needs to build more homes. But if we want to address the affordability problem Canadians are telling us matters, we need to think beyond supply alone. We need to build a housing system that makes homes easier to build—and possible to own.

Josh Hunt is the Founder and CEO of IGV Housing, an integrated housing platform making homes easier to build and possible to own.

items._ogDesc: Canadian asking rents dropped for a 24th month in September. But with units shrinking 4.2%, renters are paying less because they get less.
items.body:
Canadian rents continue to fall but a lack of demand hasn’t been the driver. Rentals.ca and Urbanation data shows asking rents fell in September. This marked a 24th straight month of declines, mostly in condo apartments. However, more than half the drop within the past two years was due to shrinking unit size.

Canadian Rents Have Dropped For 2 Years Straight

Source: Rentals.ca; Urbanation.

The average asking rent for all unit types fell for a 24th straight month to $2,034/month in September. That brings prices 4.2% lower than last year, and 9.2% (-$168) below the May 2024 peak. While last month was the weakest September since 2022, asking rents are still 16.2% higher than they were in 2021.

“According to Statistics Canada, average weekly earnings in Canada have risen by 19.4% over the past five years, indicating a general improvement in rental affordability,” explains the author of the report. However, recent Bank of Canada research shows wage gains are concentrated in older households. That’s not quite the relief suggested in the headline.

The slump is primarily in Ontario (-4.8% y/y), Manitoba (-3.2%), B.C. (-2.9%), and Alberta (-2.6%). Meanwhile, in Atlantic Canada (+3.5% y/y), where studio (0-bedroom) apartments came in a mind-boggling 34.5% higher. Inflation has also been tracking much higher on the East Coast. Clearly, rent is one of those factors.

Mom and Pop Investors Are Seeing Rents Fall Fastest

Mom and pop investors are getting a reality check. Asking rents for condo apartments fell 7.8% y/y to $2,052/month, while secondary low-rise units fell 7.4% to $2,016/month. In contrast, purpose-built units only fell 2.7% to $2,036/month over the same period.

The report didn’t dive into the reasons behind the divergence, but there are some obvious factors at play. The recent low-rate boom produced a large number of cashflow negative speculative landlords (a.k.a. speculords). They’re likely less prepared to hold out than institutions. Taxpayer-funded bailouts and loans for institutions also push the odds in their favor.

Canadian Renters Are Paying Less Because They’re Getting Less

Now for the bitter truth—landlords are asking for less because they’re providing less. The average rental unit shrank to 852 sqft in September, down 4.2% over the past two years. That explains more than half of the 7.3% drop in average asking rents over that period. A falling headline number is amplified by the shrinking apartments offered.

Falling average rents are tricky, not unlike the average income as we mentioned above. The drop is influenced more by smaller units than it’s driven by an actual correction. There’s been little progress over the past two years, and a massive disconnect still remains.
